result: Human Purkinje cells are substantially larger than previously described, with dendritic lengths of 6–7 cm (~11× longer than mouse), making them the largest neuron in the human brain. They exceed allometric constraints by cortical thickness, being ~4.5× wider but only 2.3× taller than mouse PCs, with horizontal dimensionality and more horizontal branch eccentricities. Human PCs have more branches, higher branch orders, and longer branch segments than mouse, while converging on similar thin dendrite diameters (~0.6–1 μm).
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. The editor states this is 'a convincing study of the morphological properties of Purkinje cell dendrites' and the data 'will provide an important resource.' Reviewer 1 notes 'the manuscript provides an exceptionally detailed analysis of PC morphology across species, surpassing any prior publication' with 'systematic and thorough methodology, rigorous data analysis.' Reviewer 2 states 'the authors have carried out a meticulous anatomical quantification' showing 'human PC dendrites are much larger than would be expected from straightforward scaling to brain size.' No concerns were raised about these morphological measurements.

result: Human PC spines are denser (6.9 vs 4.9 spines/μm) and larger (~0.36 vs 0.29 μm) than mouse spines, with longer necks and greater protrusion from dendrites. Both species show higher spine densities on distal dendrites. Extrapolating from dendritic length and spine density, human PCs may receive 400,000–600,000 spines compared to 30,000–40,000 in mouse, potentially upward of 1 million inputs when accounting for branched spines and spine clusters.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these spine findings. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'have largely achieved their aims, with the results effectively supporting their conclusions' and notes the work provides 'exceptionally detailed analysis.' Reviewer 2 describes 'detailed analyses of spine properties and interesting and unexpected new findings' and states the data 'will be of widespread interest to the cerebellar field.' The editor calls this 'a convincing study' of spine properties. No methodological concerns were raised about the spine density or size measurements.

result: Human PCs include a previously unreported 'spine cluster' structure not found in mouse (only 1 of 1380 mouse spines met criteria). Spine clusters are present at 0.52±0.16/μm density, increasing distally, typically with 4–6 puncta and 0.49±0.42 μm³ volume. They were observed across all human branches, cells, and specimens, including in tissue from a 37-year-old.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm this novel finding without raising concerns. Reviewer 1 notes the manuscript provides 'exceptionally detailed analysis' and 'the authors have largely achieved their aims, with the results effectively supporting their conclusions.' Reviewer 2 specifically mentions 'interesting and unexpected new findings' and states the work will be 'of widespread interest to the cerebellar field.' The editor describes this as 'a convincing study.' The observation in younger tissue (37-year-old) addresses potential age-related concerns, and no reviewer questioned the validity of this structure.

result: Non-canonical climbing fiber (CF) multi-innervation is present in adult human PCs, with at least 11% and possibly up to 50% of human PCs receiving multiple CFs (minimum rate ~15% similar to mouse). Multi-innervated cells are more multi-branched (80% Poly) and horizontally oriented (80% horizontal) than mono-innervated cells. The relationship between multi-branched structure and CF multi-innervation may be conserved across species.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 2 states 'importantly, they now present immunolabelling results that trace climbing fiber axons innervating human PCs' and notes 'the work suggests that human PCs that have two clearly distinct dendritic branches have an approximately 80% chance of receiving more than one CF input, segregated across the two branches.' Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'have largely achieved their aims, with the results effectively supporting their conclusions.' The editor calls this 'a convincing study' of 'the anatomical determinants of multi-innervation by climbing fibers.' No concerns were raised about the CF labeling or multi-innervation analysis.

result: Multi-branched PCs are more prevalent in posterior and lateral cerebellum (Crus I/II vs L5-6), co-varying with functional boundaries from a consensus atlas. Adjacent cells show nonrandom clustering by morphology (17.4% in human vs 12.6% in mouse), with clusters spanning ~537 μm (2.6 cells) in human vermis and ~838 μm in hemisphere. The spatial scale of clustering is congruent with dendritic arbor width. Regional morphological demographics align with four functional classes, with more complex morphology in regions processing cognitive and associative information.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm these regional and clustering findings. Reviewer 1 states 'the authors have largely achieved their aims, with the results effectively supporting their conclusions' and notes 'systematic and thorough methodology, rigorous data analysis.' Reviewer 2 describes the work as providing 'meticulous anatomical quantification' and states the data 'will be of widespread interest to the cerebellar field.' The editor calls this 'a convincing study.' No concerns were raised about the regional analysis or clustering methodology, and the alignment with functional boundaries is presented as a novel and interesting correlation.

result: Despite species differences, human and mouse PCs share conserved features (thin dendrite diameter, fractal branching patterns) alongside non-allometric differences. The confluence of invariant, allometric, and non-allometric features may indicate human PC physiology diverges from rodent not only in scale but in kind. Spine clusters may provide new modes of synaptic signaling and amplification. Multi-branched structure may permit enhanced input multiplexing, with human PCs potentially performing highly complex computations unlike mouse. However, expansion of input numerosity does not necessarily improve computational capacity, as seen in disease models.
evaluation: These interpretive and speculative claims receive mixed treatment. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'the work is, by necessity, purely anatomical. It remains to be seen whether there are any functional differences in ion channel expression or functional mapping of granule inputs to human PCs compared with the mouse that might mitigate the major differences in electronic properties suggested.' This indicates the functional implications are uncertain and require future validation. While reviewers accept the anatomical observations, the mechanistic and computational interpretations are acknowledged as hypotheses requiring further testing.

result: Human PCs are genetically diverse with four developmental subtypes identified by transcriptomics, with subtype ratios shifted in mammalian evolution. Human-specific PC genes have been suggested. PC morphology and CF signaling are altered in disease models (spinocerebellar ataxia, autism, essential tremor, Friedreich's ataxia). Previously reported human PC dendritic length was 10–20,000 μm, which would suggest PCs are similar in size to pyramidal cells.
evaluation: These claims are primarily based on citations to prior literature and are presented as established context. Reviewers do not challenge these background statements. Reviewer 1 notes the manuscript 'surpasses any prior publication' in its analysis, implicitly accepting the characterization of previous work as limited. Reviewer 2 acknowledges the work 'follows up on a previously published paper' and accepts the prior findings as context. The disease-related claims are cited references that reviewers do not dispute.

result: Background context: PCs are the sole cerebellar cortical output, receiving tens of thousands of parallel fiber inputs and climbing fiber prediction-error signals. PCs are classically seen as stereotypical but are morphologically diverse in mouse, with multi-branched PCs receiving non-canonical CF multi-innervation. PC dendrites show heterogeneous excitability and can undergo independent compartment-level plasticity. Human PC morphology has been analyzed only occasionally in small numbers since Golgi and Ramón y Cajal, with very little known about human PC physiology.
evaluation: These introductory and contextual claims are well-established in the field and supported by extensive citations. Reviewers do not challenge any of these background statements. Reviewer 2 explicitly acknowledges 'this manuscript follows up on a previously published paper' and accepts the prior characterization of PC diversity and multi-innervation in mouse. Reviewer 1 notes the current work 'surpasses any prior publication' in its analysis of human PCs, implicitly accepting the characterization of limited prior knowledge. These claims provide accepted scientific context for the study.

result: Nonrandom spatial clustering of neuronal cells by morphological subtype has not previously been described in other brain areas, potentially making this a cerebellum-specific means to boost functional diversity.
evaluation: This claim about the novelty and uniqueness of morphological clustering is not explicitly evaluated by reviewers. While reviewers affirm the clustering findings themselves (see result on C66-C77), they do not comment on whether this phenomenon is truly unprecedented in other brain regions or whether it is cerebellum-specific. This represents a broader interpretive claim about the significance and uniqueness of the finding that was not directly addressed in the reviews.
